walkthroughs.body_html: Holderness SMP: hold the line at settlements (Bridlington, Hornsea, Withernsea, Mappleton); no active intervention along rural cliffs; managed realignment at Spurn. Decisions reflect cost-benefit: defending farmland uneconomic at £2 million/km vs cost of relocating settlements.

1991: £2 million two rock groynes plus rip-rap to protect B1242 road and village (50 houses). Successful at Mappleton but caused 1.8 m/yr increased erosion at Cowden, 3 km south, losing farmland and a holiday park. Demonstrates sediment cell connectivity in management decisions.

Property owners want defences; ecologists support natural retreat; council balances limited budget. Sue Earle (Skipsea, lost home 2017) campaigned for buy-out scheme. Coastal Change Pathfinder grants provided £11 million UK-wide 2009-11 but failed to scale.

mcqs.q: Why might managed retreat be more sustainable than building a sea wall?
options: It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.
Managed retreat means letting all coastal towns disappear into the sea.
Sea walls always solve coastal erosion problems permanently.
Sea walls are expensive, deflect erosion elsewhere and reflect wave energy worsening beach loss; managed retreat works with natural processes, creates habitat and is cheaper long-term.

mcqs.q: Why are cities warmer than surrounding countryside?
options: Because cities are always in warmer climates.
It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.
Dark surfaces absorb solar radiation, concrete and brick store heat, vehicles and buildings release heat, and lack of vegetation reduces cooling by evapotranspiration.
Because cities are closer to the sun due to tall buildings.
